notes.title: How the cuisine filters were policed
notes.body: Every food card names a specific dish or beer — a label alone doesn’t qualify. The Ghent canon: waterzooi, Gentse stoverij, the cuberdon (neuzekes), Tierenteyn mustard and a strong veg bench — with the Gruut brewery and jenever at ’t Dreupelkot. Beer & breweries are their own grouped layer. A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it serves.

notes.title: Web-searched in-language and fact-checked
notes.body: Every place is traceable to a credible source — Michelin, UNESCO, Gault&Millau, De Standaard, Het Nieuwsblad, VRT NWS, Visit Gent, beer authorities and vetted local creators — recorded in data/sources.json. Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked open. Yelp/TripAdvisor/RateBeer never count toward the two-source bar.

places.n: Gravensteen (Kasteel van de Graven van Vlaanderen)
places.w: The moated 12th-century castle of the Counts of Flanders in the very heart of the city — a rare intact medieval fortress with ramparts, towers and a torture-instrument collection, reached over its own drawbridge.

Ghent's cathedral houses the world's most famous polyptych, Hubert and Jan van Eyck's 'Adoration of the Mystic Lamb' (Het Lam Gods, 1432) — still on view in situ, with a state-of-the-art visitor centre. The lower church and crypt add centuries of art.

The 91-metre 14th-century belfry, a UNESCO World Heritage 'Belfry of Belgium and France', crowned by a gilded dragon; the middle tower of Ghent's famous three-tower row, with a glass lift to a panoramic viewing gallery.
The medieval inner harbour on the Leie, lined with guild houses spanning Romanesque to Baroque; Ghent's most photographed quays and, at dusk, the city's living room for a drink by the water.
A cobbled alley opened to street artists in 1995 and repainted constantly — a free, ever-changing open-air gallery a few steps from the City Hall. You never see the same walls twice.
A pocket of winding medieval lanes and cobbles behind the Gravensteen — once a tanners' and weavers' quarter, now Ghent's most atmospheric restaurant-and-café district.

Ghent's grand civic square, site of markets, joyous entries and bloody guild battles for seven centuries; at its centre the 1863 bronze of Jacob van Artevelde pointing toward England. The 14th-century Toreken guildhouse stands on the corner.
A pure example of Scheldt Gothic in blue Tournai stone, built from the 13th century by the merchants of the Graslei and dedicated to St Nicholas, patron of traders. The first of Ghent's three towers.
Ghent's museum of contemporary art, built by Jan Hoet into an international name — post-war and living artists from Bacon and Broodthaers to Panamarenko, with restlessly changing shows.
The Fine Arts Museum in Citadelpark: six centuries from Hieronymus Bosch and the Flemish Primitives to Ensor and the Symbolists, in a serene neoclassical building.
The city museum set in the medieval Bijloke abbey and hospital, telling Ghent's story from Roman settlement to today — including a walk-on aerial photo of the whole city.
The stone bridge that frames Ghent's picture-postcard view — Graslei, Korenlei and the three towers all in one sweep. The single best free vantage point in the city.
Ghent's City Hall wears two faces on one block: flamboyant Late Gothic and sober Renaissance. Inside, the Pacificatiezaal recalls the 1576 Pacification of Ghent.
A 15th-century covered meat market with a soaring timber roof, once where all the city's meat was inspected; now a showcase and tasting hall for East-Flemish regional products.
A 12,500-kg wrought-iron bombard of the 15th century, five metres long — one of the largest siege guns of the Middle Ages, nicknamed the 'Mad Meg'. It stands on the square that bears its name.
An international design collection from Art Nouveau and Art Deco to contemporary, spanning an 18th-century mansion and a bold new wing.
Henry van de Velde's modernist library tower for Ghent University (1930s–40s), a listed monument of stripped concrete recently restored, with a belvedere over the city.

A walled 13th-century beguinage of whitewashed houses, church and garden around a green — founded c.1234 by Joanna of Constantinople and inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List of Flemish Beguinages.
A museum of everyday 20th-century life set in Ghent's last surviving almshouse — reconstructed interiors, home movies and objects of ordinary Flemish lives, around a quiet courtyard.
A Benedictine abbey founded in the 7th century by St Amandus, with a Baroque church, a vineyard garden and ruins, now the Kunsthal Sint-Pietersabdij exhibition space.
The socialist cooperative's 1913 festival hall, an eclectic Art Nouveau/Art Deco monument by Ferdinand Dierkens — reopened in 2026 after a major restoration as a landmark arts centre and café.
Ghent's award-winning riverside library and knowledge centre (2017), a striking angular building where the Schelde meets the city — free to enter, with terraces over the water.
A quay of richly carved Baroque façades facing the water — 'De Fluitspeler'/'Het Vliegend Hert' (1669) and the 'House of the Seven Works of Mercy' among the finest reliefs in the city.

The old fish market at the confluence of Leie and Lieve, its gate crowned by a Baroque Neptune; fish was sold here from the Middle Ages to the 1960s, now a brasserie and event venue facing the Gravensteen.
Set in Belgium's first purpose-built psychiatric hospital (1850s), a museum on the history of psychiatry and the shifting line between 'mad' and 'normal', with a notable outsider-art collection.
Machines, people and the textile boom that made Ghent the 'Manchester of the continent', in a canalside former cotton mill — working looms and the story of industrial labour.
A vast neo-Gothic beguinage village of some 80 houses and a central church, built 1873–76 when the beguines left the old city centre; UNESCO World Heritage and still remarkably intact.

A 13th-century Scheldt-Gothic stone castle named for the swarthy knight Geeraard 'the Devil' — over the centuries an armoury, monastery, seminary, asylum and prison, now a striking waterside landmark.
The evocative ruins of the abbey where Ghent was born — cloister, refectory and lapidary museum of stone fragments, at the old confluence of Leie and Schelde.
The city's largest 19th-century park — winding paths, a grotto, bandstand and, at its edge, the university's botanical garden with tropical glasshouses. Home to MSK and S.M.A.K.
Ghent's daily flower market on its most elegant square, at its liveliest on Sunday mornings when a brass kiosk plays and locals take an oyster-and-white-wine aperitif.
A restored inner-city marina at the historic meeting of the rivers, ringed by cafés — Ghent's spot for a canoe or an electric boat and a swim at the Van Eyck baths nearby.
A twin-towered 15th-century water gate that once defended the city's canals — a squat, castle-like brick landmark giving its name to the surrounding neighbourhood.

places.n: De Wereld van Kina: het Huis
places.w: A family nature-and-science museum — cabinets of animals, minerals and the human body, plus a botanical garden across town — the former Michel Thiery school museum.
A Romanesque-to-Gothic church with two western towers, at the heart of the Bij Sint-Jacobs square famed for its weekend flea market and its nightlife.
A cluster of medieval patrician 'stone houses' of the van der Sickelen family around a hidden galleried courtyard — the 'lovers' corner' — now part of the conservatory.
A 13th-century Cistercian hospital and abbey complex with a magnificent painted timber ceiling, now the Bijloke music centre — one of Ghent's most beautiful medieval ensembles.
The legendary music café and dance hall on the Vlasmarkt, epicentre of Ghent nightlife and the subject of Felix Van Groeningen's 2016 film 'Belgica'.

Ghent's central square where the old grain market stood, ringed by the former post office, the Sint-Niklaaskerk and pavement cafés — the natural starting point for the tower row and the historic core.
A compact medieval market square wedged between the Groot Vleeshuis and the Leie — home to Tierenteyn's mustard shop, the rival cuberdon carts and the city's oldest bakery. Ghent's edible heart.
Ghent University's ceremonial hall of 1826, a neoclassical temple with a Pantheon-inspired portico of eight Corinthian columns — the building in the UGent logo, by city architect Lodewijk Roelandt.
A monumental 19th-century church in a rare Romano-Byzantine revival style, its vast interior richly decorated with murals and marble — one of Ghent's grandest and least-expected sacred spaces.

A moated Flemish-Renaissance water castle in a loop of the Leie south of Ghent — stepped gables, onion domes and a lavishly furnished interior, set in a 45-hectare park still inhabited by the same family.
The riverside village that gave its name to two schools of Flemish art — a postcard of the Leie, willows and whitewashed farms that drew Minne, Van de Woestyne, Permeke and the Latem expressionists.
An internationally regarded museum of modern and contemporary art in Deurle, founded on the Dhondt-Dhaenens collection of Flemish masters and now known for adventurous temporary shows.

places.n: mudel — Museum van Deinze en de Leiestreek
places.w: Deinze's fine-arts and folklore museum, holding the region's richest collection of Leie-school painting — Emile Claus, Permeke, Gustave Van de Woestyne, Roger Raveel — alongside local ethnography.
The house and studio of Flemish expressionist Gust De Smet, kept as he left it, with his paintings in the setting where they were made — one of Deurle's cluster of artist-museums.
The former home and studio of painter Edgard Gevaert on a three-hectare domain, showing work by nearly all the great Latem artists — George Minne, Servaes, Valerius de Saedeleer.
A small Deurle museum devoted to luminist painter Leon De Smet, Gust's brother — intimate portraits and interiors, open on a limited basis.
The village's small parish church, a place of quiet that also holds art treasures by Latem masters Gustave Van de Woestyne and George Minne.
The water meadows and willow-lined bends of the Leie that the Latem painters immortalised — a flat, luminous walking and cycling landscape, with a route tracing the very spots in their canvases.

A crisp white Stéphane Beel building in the artist's home village, one of the few Belgian artists to get his own museum in his lifetime — 300+ paintings and 550 drawings by the post-war master Roger Raveel.
A free 27-hectare provincial park in the heart of Deinze between the Leie and the Schipdonk canal — playgrounds, a petting farm with deer and donkeys, mini-golf and riverside walks.

Ghent's most famous beer café, with the city's largest Belgian-beer list (500+). Order the 1.2-litre house boot and you hand over a shoe as deposit, hoisted to the ceiling in a basket until you return the glass.
A canalside brown pub in a former riverside house with a waterfront terrace and around 175 beers, including its own Klokke Roeland. The classic Ghent beer stop, next to its jenever annex.
A tiny jenever house on the water beside the Waterhuis, pouring only genever — over 200 kinds, from cactus to vanilla to chocolate — served ice-cold and brimful.
Annick De Splenter's city brewery revives 'gruut' — a medieval herb blend used instead of hops — in five house beers plus a rotating 'Maîtresse'. Tours and a canalside brewery bar in the centre.
A vast beer specialty shop and bar that commissions its own Gentse Tripel, alongside a huge range of Belgian and international beers, wines and spirits — the go-to for beer to take home.
A characterful troll-themed beer café by Sint-Jacobs with a deep, well-kept list of trappist and abbey beers and a quiet upstairs — a beer-lover's classic away from the tourist crush.
A historic pub in a former granary right in the centre, with two terraces — one on the bustling street, one over the Leie — and a solid local beer list.
By far the smallest café in Ghent, an 18th-century brown pub on the Groentenmarkt pouring its own Galgenbier — squeeze in upstairs or take a stool on the market.
One of the last genuine brown cafés in the centre — candlelit, chamber-pots on the ceiling, a 1667 building full of stories in the heart of Patershol. Beer and conversation, nothing else.
An authentic Patershol brasserie that does the Ghent classics properly — creamy waterzooi of farm chicken and beef stoverij braised in beer — in a warm, cosy room.
A typical Ghent brasserie in a striking black-and-white room directly below St Bavo's, with a big summer terrace on the square — the reliable address for stoverij and waterzooi in the centre.
A grand belle-époque brasserie in a converted warehouse down an atmospheric alley — oysters, seafood and French-Italian classics under a soaring iron-and-glass roof.
An open-kitchen canteen serving one thing brilliantly: handmade meatballs with a molten filling, from honestly sourced meat, with mash and greens. Walk-in, no reservations.
A brasserie set in the Baroque old fish market at the foot of the Gravensteen, with a waterside terrace where the Leie and Lieve meet — classic dishes in one of Ghent's most scenic rooms.
Chef Michaël Vrijmoed's two-Michelin-star restaurant, Ghent's culinary summit — precise, produce-driven tasting menus with a celebrated cellar.
Chef Olly Ceulenaere's one-star restaurant, quietly one of Belgium's most influential kitchens — a set surprise menu built around vegetables, ferments and Flemish produce.
Chef Marcelo Ballardin's one-star OAK — contemporary, personal cooking with surprising combinations, on a quiet street near the Gravensteen.
Vilhjalmur Sigurdarson's intimate restaurant, holder of a Michelin Green Star for sustainable gastronomy — a tight seasonal menu rooted in Flemish and Nordic produce.
A refined modern-French, farm-to-table table in Patershol, selected by the Michelin Guide — a small, chef-led room with a strong seasonal menu.
A Michelin-listed Patershol restaurant serving modern, creative Belgian cooking in a relaxed room — 3–4-course lunches, longer tasting menus at night.
Chef Tom Pauweleyn's warm neighbourhood gastro-bistro, named Gault&Millau's Gastro-Bistro of the Year 2025 — creative, generous cooking off a lively square.
A long-loved Gault&Millau restaurant on the banks of the Leie south of the centre, with a waterside terrace — refined seasonal cooking away from the crowds.
The Ghent institution that claims to have invented the broodje Martino — spicy raw-beef préparé — still serving it, plus its famous cheese-egg-burger, in a no-frills snackbar since decades.
Ghent's pioneering veg restaurant, open since 1996 and now fully vegan — burgers, bowls and daily specials that helped make the city Europe's self-styled veggie capital.
An organic plant-based canteen — buddha bowls, whole-food sushi, tonic wines — small, warm and central; the Ghent original of a concept now exported worldwide.
A daylight bistro named for its ecological, local-produce philosophy — seasonal, largely vegetable-forward plates by the Glazen Straatje.
A long-running vegetarian restaurant in a stepped-gable house opposite the Gravensteen, with a garden terrace — organic, seasonal lunches, a Ghent veggie fixture.
A gentle lunch spot known for its generous, mostly-vegan buffet — spreads, salads and warm dishes that change with the season and the market.
Two rival carts side by side on the Groentenmarkt sell Ghent's raspberry cone-sweets, the cuberdon or 'neuzeke' — a decades-long feud (the viral 'war of the noses') that has become city folklore.

A mustard shop unchanged since the 19th century, making Ghent's pungent mustard on the premises and scooping it, still fizzing, from a cellar barrel into stoneware pots before your eyes. Founded 1790.
A tiny, much-loved patisserie and breakfast spot on the Kraanlei overlooking the water — cheesecakes, pies and homemade granola in a doll's-house room.
Nicolas Vanaise's minimalist chocolate boutique, among Belgium's most admired — pralines built on unexpected flavours like yuzu, tonka, truffle and pepper. In the Gault&Millau chocolatier guide.
A cosy coffee roastery in the heart of Ghent since 1937 — dark, nostalgic and beloved by locals as much as visitors for a proper espresso.
A colourful 1904 Art Nouveau corner housing a welcoming specialty coffee bar and B&B on the edge of Patershol — organic, locally sourced, run by a British owner who fell for the city.
A coffee-and-bicycle bar near Portus Ganda where you sip a cappuccino among collectible bikes and gear — a cheerful spot on the water for cyclists and caffeine.
The Ghent bar of Belgian specialty roaster OR Coffee (founded here in 2009) — expertly pulled coffee, organic bread and cake, near the university quarter.
Kobe Desramaults' bakery-restaurant — sourdough, wood-fired pizza and brunch from a Scandinavian oven — voted the country's best new concept when it opened and still a hotspot.
A student-belt frituur repeatedly voted Ghent's best, famed for crisp fries and an unusually broad range of vegetarian and vegan snacks.
A central frituur beside St Michael's, frying in vegetable oil with a wide vegetarian and vegan range — fries with a canal view.
A near-legendary frituur at the top of student-nightlife street Overpoort, credited with inventing the 'julientje' — the late-night fix every Ghent student knows, meals under ten euros.

A hip wood-fired pizzeria between the Gravensteen and the Groentenmarkt whose dough is raised with Duvel yeast — 'otomat' with red sauce, 'notomat' white; you can even moor a boat and order to the quay. In the Gault&Millau guide.
A creative, seasonal neighbourhood restaurant near Dampoort with a Gault&Millau score — tight lunch and multi-course dinner menus in a warm room off the tourist track.
A homely coffee-and-cake bar with organic artisan bread, art on the walls and a famous apple pie — a Ghent favourite for take-away or a slow morning by the Zuivelbrug.
A small order-at-the-counter veggie eatery a few blocks from the Gravensteen — multigrain veggie burgers, sweet-potato fries and thick shakes; a long-running Ghent meat-free staple.
Ghent's oldest bakery, baking in a 17th-century cellar workshop on the Groentenmarkt — tiny, nostalgic and known for mastellen and warm sausage rolls.
A café, concert hall and gallery run by the non-profit that relaunched the Gentse Feesten in 1970 — beers, live music and a terrace on the Sint-Jacobs square, open every day.

A stylish, long-established brasserie in the artists' village — simple but refined cooking from the freshest produce (olive oil, organic meat, shellfish) and a phenomenal cellar. In the Michelin Guide.
A lively Sint-Martens-Latem brasserie whose cooking has gained focus and refinement — a second Gault&Millau toque and a place in the Michelin Guide.
A Michelin-listed Sint-Martens-Latem restaurant serving traditional, generous cooking in a converted barn — a Leie-region classic.
A refined riverside hotel-restaurant in Deurle right on the Leie, with a coveted summer terrace over the water — the region's classic address for a long lunch by the river.
A comfortable Gault&Millau restaurant in a quiet green setting between the village square of Bachte and the banks of the Oude Leie, near Ooidonk Castle.
A well-regarded Gault&Millau restaurant in Deinze serving polished seasonal cooking, on the avenue named for painter Emile Claus.
A Gault&Millau restaurant on the banks of the Leie in Deinze, with a terrace over the water and a market-driven seasonal menu.
A Gault&Millau bistro in central Deinze offering honest, well-executed dishes in a relaxed setting.
An intimate, cosy café-restaurant near Ooidonk in Bachte-Maria-Leerne, listed by Gault&Millau — a relaxed stop on a Leie-valley outing.
